body:
@annevk Its perhaps the fact that our URL parsing is trying to support more than strictly the WHATWG notion of hosts, and trying to figure out when/how those are canonicalized as such. I would be surprised if @achristensen07 doesn't run into a similar issue re: NSURL.

For example, I recently was asked to look into having `GURL` (our internal URL representation that serves as our parser/canonicalizer) support `smb://` URL parsing (not for the intent of web exposure), and to support the NetBIOS naming scheme. We're not keen to bifurcate URL parsing/canonicalization more than absolutely necessary (i.e. we're not keen to have entirely separate parse/canonicalization for Web vs Chrome usages of URLs). The same nominally applies to things like `chrome-extension` or other UA-extended schemes.

Even within the space of certificates, during certificate linting, it was highlighted that UAs' notion of IDNs and RFC 5280s notions are non-aligned - see specifically [RFC 5280, Section 7.2](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5280#section-7.2) and note well the use of [RFC 3490](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3490), the reference to which was explicitly not updated to point to [RFC 5890](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5890) or [RFC 5891](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5891)

I think for host, treating it as opaque (but defining the character space and escaping rules) is a desirable goal, but acknowledge that holds a host of issues regarding U-Label vs A-Label and determining when IDN policies apply.

A way out here mentioned in https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1184059#c29 might be that we have a separate "DNS domain" definition which is effectively a further validation on the output of the host parser (if it is a domain) that allows

* what https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc1034 as modified by https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc1123#section-2 allows
* underscores
* hyphens in more places?

As this definition is mainly needed by various networking standards, it doesn't necessarily have to live in the URL Standard. Fetch could be a place, but perhaps filing some issues against the relevant standards that have a dependency on the "broken" concept could also result in some action.

I wrote a web-platform-tests test (https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/65470, currently a draft) to find out which hosts browsers are willing to request once the URL parser has accepted them.

For Chrome and Firefox every request went through wptserve as a proxy (using a PAC file), so no DNS was involved and the results reflect the browser's own check. Both run that same check before a normal DNS lookup. For Safari, requests went through a real lookup by the macOS resolver, pointed at wptserve's DNS server, so a failure there can come from Safari or from macOS.

| Host | Chrome 160 | Firefox 161 | Safari 27.3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| ASCII alphanumerics, `-` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `_` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `$`, `+` | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| ``! " & ' ( ) * , ; = ` { } ~`` | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Leading or trailing `-` or `_`, labels consisting of only `-` or `_`, `ab--c` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Last label starting with `-` or `_` | ❌ | ✅ | not tested |
| Last label ending with `-` or `_` | ✅ | ✅ | not tested |
| Empty label (`a..b`, `.a.b`, `a.b..`) | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Trailing dot | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| 63-code-point label | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| 64-code-point label | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| 253 code points | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| 254 code points | ❌ | ❌ | ✅¹ |
| 254 code points, including a trailing dot | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| 255 code points, including a trailing dot | ❌ | ❌ | ✅¹ |

¹ macOS sent the DNS query even though the name exceeds DNS's 255-octet limit. wptserve's DNS server couldn't answer for a name that long, so the request itself never completed.

Observations:

* All three accept ASCII alphanumerics, `-`, and `_`. None of them restrict where `-` and `_` can appear, except that Chrome requires the last label to start with an ASCII alphanumeric.
* Firefox also accepts `$` and `+`. Safari accepts every ASCII code point the host parser allows in a domain.
* Chrome rejects empty labels, labels longer than 63 code points, and hosts longer than 253 code points (254 with a trailing dot). Safari also rejects empty labels and labels longer than 63 code points, but doesn't limit the total length. Firefox only limits the total length, to 253 code points with any trailing dot included, and leaves the rest to the resolver.

The checks are `IsCanonicalizedHostCompliant()` in Chromium (`net/base/url_util.cc`) and `net_IsValidDNSHost()` in Gecko (`netwerk/base/nsURLHelper.cpp`).

So a "DNS domain" concept along the lines of https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/397#issuecomment-605031328 (LDH plus `_`, with hyphens allowed anywhere) would match Chrome, but would be stricter than Firefox and considerably stricter than Safari.

One difference here, which you may be aware of, but I think is good to take note of as we figure out how to better align behavior, is that Chrome will create URLs with many hosts it considers non-compliant, only applying host string restrictions based on the general URL spec, but will refuse to fetch them, instead of refusing to construct the URL at all.

I think it does actually reject URLs with HTTP[S] hosts with a numeric final label that aren't IPv4 addresses, and validates IPv6 address format as well, but is fairly permissive outside of that.

The specification's URL parser has those same restrictions. Though Chrome still has some failures per https://wpt.fyi/results/url, but not sure if those are for hosts or elsewhere.

To your larger point, yes, this should maybe be moved to the Fetch repository. I haven't quite determined what if anything we want to do here yet, but it might make sense to validate hosts before we send them over the network as Chromium and Gecko are doing.
